trial_name: TiP-Ex — PSV vs T-Piece SBT in High-Risk ICU Patients (2022)
journal: The New England Journal of Medicine
citation: Thille AW, Gacouin A, Coudroy R, et al. Spontaneous-Breathing Trials with Pressure-Support Ventilation or a T-Piece. N Engl J Med. 2022;387:1843-54.
trial_type: RCT — multicenter, pragmatic, parallel-group, open-label, superiority
one_liner: In high-risk ICU patients, a PSV-based SBT strategy did not increase ventilator-free days at day 28 compared with a T-piece strategy, despite improving initial SBT success and reducing prolonged weaning.

pico.population: Adult ICU patients at high risk of extubation failure (age >65 years and/or chronic cardiac/respiratory disease), invasively ventilated for >24 hours and ready for an initial SBT.
pico.intervention: 1-hour SBT with pressure-support ventilation (PSV 8 cmH2O, PEEP 0 cmH2O).
pico.comparison: 1-hour SBT with a T-piece (oxygen flow 4–6 L/min).

background.existing_knowledge: SBTs are a core readiness test before extubation, but the tested conditions vary (T-piece, low-level PSV, CPAP). T-piece SBTs remove ventilator assistance but retain ETT load; PSV SBTs add inspiratory assistance, potentially reducing work of breathing.
background.knowledge_gap: Prior studies suggested PSV may increase SBT success and accelerate extubation, but concerns persisted that an easier test could permit premature extubation and increase reintubation, especially in high-risk patients.
background.hypothesis: In high-risk mechanically ventilated adults deemed ready for extubation assessment, a PSV-based SBT strategy (vs a T-piece SBT strategy) would increase ventilator-free days at day 28, without worsening clinically important harms such as reintubation.

methods.design: Multicentre, investigator-initiated, pragmatic, parallel-group, randomised controlled superiority trial; open-label with central web-based randomisation stratified by centre (block size 4).

inclusion: Intubated and invasively ventilated for >24 hours.
High-risk: Age >65 years and/or chronic cardiac disease and/or chronic respiratory disease.

Readiness for initial SBT: Respiratory rate ≤35 breaths/min; SpO2 ≥90% with FIO2 ≤40% and PEEP ≤8 cmH2O (or PaO2/FIO2 ≥150 with PEEP ≤8); adequate cough; awake (RASS -2 to +1); no continuous sedation; no vasopressors or minimal doses.
exclusion: Do-not-reintubate decision at time of initial SBT.
Already performed an initial SBT since intubation.
Other protocol exclusions (e.g., legal protections/consent constraints).

methods.intervention: PSV SBT strategy: 1-hour SBT on the ventilator with PSV 8 cmH2O and PEEP 0 cmH2O (target FIO2 ≤0.40). After SBT success, extubation recommended as soon as possible after ~1 hour rest. If SBT failure, return to ventilatory support; repeat SBT daily until success.
methods.comparison: T-piece SBT strategy: 1-hour SBT with a T-piece, using oxygen flow 4–6 L/min (target FIO2 ≤0.40). Same extubation encouragement and repeat-testing approach as intervention.
methods.blinding: Unblinded (clinicians and patients). Extubation timing and post-extubation supports were clinician-driven.
methods.sample_size_power: 900 patients required to detect an absolute increase of 2 ventilator-free days at day 28 (two-sided alpha 0.05; 80% power); planned sample size increased to 1000 to allow for exclusions.
methods.primary_outcome: Ventilator-free days at day 28 (death counted as 0 days).
secondary_outcomes: Days alive without invasive or non-invasive ventilation at day 28
Median time to extubation after successful initial SBT
Simple weaning (extubation <24 h after initial SBT)
Prolonged weaning (>7 days after initial SBT)
Extubation after one SBT without reintubation within 72 h
methods.follow_up: 28 days for the primary outcome; 90 days for mortality and longer-term outcomes.

headline_bullets: PSV SBTs increased initial SBT success (79.1% vs 71.7%) and reduced prolonged weaning (>7 days: 2.3% vs 5.6%).
No difference in the primary outcome of ventilator-free days at day 28 (median 27 vs 27; median difference 0; 95% CI -0.5 to 1; P=0.31).
Reintubation ≤7 days was similar (14.9% vs 13.6%), and 90-day mortality was similar (16.5% vs 18.7%).
Hypercapnic coma as a reintubation indication occurred only in the PSV arm (7/78 vs 0/71; P=0.01), a signal warranting cautious interpretation.

safety: Hypercapnic coma as a reason for reintubation in ICU: 7/78 (9.0%) in PSV arm vs 0/71 (0%) in T-piece arm (P=0.01). Multiple reasons per patient; denominator = reintubated in ICU.

domains.notes: Central, web-based randomisation stratified by centre with concealed allocation (block size 4). Post-randomisation eligibility validation by a blinded committee; 969/983 (98.6%) retained for the primary analysis.

Open-label intervention; clinicians knew assignment and determined timing of extubation and adjunctive supports. Primary outcome and reintubation are largely objective, but decisions can be susceptible to expectation.

14/983 randomised patients were excluded after randomisation (6 PSV; 8 T-piece), including deaths before SBT, withdrawals, self-extubation, transfer before initial SBT, and missing data. This is a modified intention-to-treat population and could introduce bias.

Crossovers were uncommon: 6/484 (1.2%) in the PSV arm received at least one T-piece SBT; 10/485 (2.1%) in the T-piece arm received at least one PSV SBT. Mean SBT settings achieved separation consistent with the protocol.

Groups were broadly balanced in illness severity and comorbidity burden (e.g., age 69±9 vs 68±9; SAPS II 53±17 vs 53±18; chronic cardiac disease 46.9% vs 48.2%; chronic respiratory disease 24.8% vs 27.0%). A substantial minority had COVID-19 (23.3% vs 24.5%).

internal_validity.verdict: Overall, internal validity appears moderate to strong: randomisation and allocation concealment were robust and crossovers were rare, with clear separation in initial SBT success; the main limitations arise from the open-label nature of the intervention, post-randomisation eligibility exclusions, and reliance on a bounded composite primary endpoint sensitive to distributional ceiling effects.

domains.notes: Enrolled a broadly defined 'high-risk' cohort (age >65 and/or chronic cardiorespiratory disease) with a median of 6 days of ventilation before initial SBT. Exclusions and non-enrolment were substantial: of 1,476 eligible, 381 were not randomised due to staff unavailability/logistics and 112 declined participation.

31 French ICUs during the COVID-19 era; high use of prophylactic NIV/HFNC after extubation (78.3% overall among extubated patients). PSV 8 cmH2O with PEEP 0 and 1-hour duration may not match local norms. Exclusion of traumatic brain injury and neuromuscular disease limits direct extrapolation to neurocritical care.

external_validity.verdict: Generalisability is moderate: findings are highly relevant to adult ICUs caring for older patients with cardiorespiratory comorbidity, particularly where prophylactic NIV/HFNC is commonly used, but may not fully extend to resource-limited settings, neurocritical care populations, or ICUs using substantially different SBT settings/durations.

strengths: Pragmatic multicentre RCT in a clinically important, high-risk extubation population.
Clear operationalisation of SBT strategies (fixed 1-hour duration; PSV 8/PEEP 0 vs T-piece), producing measurable intervention separation.
High retention into the primary analysis (969/983 randomised) and low crossover.
Use of ventilator-free days at day 28 provides a patient-centred composite balancing earlier extubation against potential harm from reintubation and death.
limitations: Open-label design with clinician-determined extubation and reintubation decisions, potentially introducing performance bias.
Post-randomisation eligibility exclusions create a modified intention-to-treat analysis set.
Primary outcome distribution was heavily bounded (median 27/28 days in both arms), reducing sensitivity to detect operationally important but small differences in liberation timing.

High prevalence of post-extubation prophylactic respiratory support may have reduced event rates and interacted with the SBT strategy, limiting transportability to ICUs with different extubation support practices.
Secondary outcomes were not adjusted for multiplicity; many p values were not reported, limiting inferential certainty for secondary signals such as hypercapnic coma as a reintubation reason.

critical_appraisal.summary: A well-conducted pragmatic trial with moderate to strong internal validity, limited primarily by its open-label design and a primary endpoint that suffered from a ceiling effect, which may have obscured clinically meaningful differences in weaning processes.
strengths: Low crossover and high protocol adherence.
weaknesses: Open-label design introduces potential for performance bias.
Post-randomisation exclusions create a modified ITT analysis.
Primary outcome's ceiling effect limits sensitivity.

sections.authors_conclusion: In high-risk patients, a PSV-based SBT strategy improved the probability of passing the initial SBT and reduced prolonged weaning, but did not translate into more ventilator-free days or lower reintubation; either strategy can be defended as clinically acceptable when embedded in a protocolised liberation pathway.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: This trial does not mandate a change in practice but supports flexibility in SBT modality choice. PSV SBTs are a reasonable alternative to T-piece SBTs in high-risk patients, as they improve process metrics without worsening patient-centred outcomes.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: High-risk adult ICU patients (age >65 and/or chronic cardiac/respiratory disease) in settings with protocolised liberation pathways and ready access to post-extubation respiratory support (NIV/HFNC).
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: PSV SBTs are superior to T-piece SBTs for improving ventilator-free days or survival. The choice of SBT modality should not override adherence to a structured weaning and extubation protocol.
implementation_caveats: The PSV settings used (8 cmH2O, PEEP 0) may not be directly transferable to units using different 'low-level' PSV settings.
The high rate of prophylactic post-extubation NIV (78.3%) in this trial is a key contextual factor; results may differ in settings where this is not standard practice.
The signal for hypercapnic coma in the PSV arm warrants awareness, though it is not a confirmed causal harm.

controversies.notes: The median ventilator-free days at day 28 was 27 (IQR near the upper bound) in both arms, raising concerns that a bounded composite outcome may have limited sensitivity to detect differences in extubation timing; this issue was explicitly highlighted in post-publication correspondence.

The accompanying editorial emphasised that the reintubation signal and other outcomes should be interpreted in the context of modern, protocolised care (including frequent prophylactic NIV/HFNC), which can reduce extubation failure rates and potentially attenuate the effect of the SBT strategy.

The published trial protocol anticipated an absolute increase of 2 ventilator-free days at day 28 and powered the study accordingly; the observed distribution concentrated near the maximum suggests that future weaning trials may require alternative primary outcomes (e.g., time-to-successful extubation) or different analytic strategies for bounded composites.

context_related_trials.trial: Prior large RCT comparing PSV vs T-piece SBTs in a mixed-risk ICU population
context_related_trials.relation: Found higher rates of successful extubation with PSV without a clear increase in reintubation, supporting PSV as a reasonable approach in many settings; TiP-Ex suggests that in high-risk patients, the process benefits of PSV do not necessarily translate into improved ventilator-free days.

unresolved_questions: What is the optimal primary endpoint for future weaning trials to avoid ceiling effects?
Does the SBT strategy interact with the type and intensity of post-extubation respiratory support?
Is the signal for hypercapnic coma with PSV SBTs a true effect, and if so, what is the mechanism?

numbers_to_remember: Primary outcome (VFDs at day 28): 27 vs 27 (median difference 0; P=0.31)
quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: In high-risk ICU patients, a PSV SBT improves weaning process metrics but does not increase ventilator-free days or reduce reintubation compared to a T-piece SBT, supporting flexibility in SBT modality choice within a protocolised liberation pathway.
